episodes.209935: A front lifted into the area on the 3rd of March and then continued to ripple through the region over the next couple of days. Rain initially spread southwest to northeast across the area on the afternoon of the 3rd, then the focus of moderate to heavy rain became more confined to southeast Ohio and north central West Virginia during the evening and overnight hours. Another wave of showers pushed across the area after daybreak, however precipitation amounts were fairly light. A lull in precipitation occurred mid to late morning, then precipitation began streaming back into the area from the west during the afternoon.||In the first twenty-four hours of the event, precipitation amounts ranged from around half an inch to two inches across northern West Virginia. Meanwhile, amounts generally remained under an inch within the southern half of the state. Highest amounts were observed in a narrow swath across Wood, Jackson, Wirt, Ritchie, Calhoun, and Gilmer counties. Another one to two and a half inches of rain fell across portions of the state as additional rounds of rain, and some thunderstorms, traversed the area into the morning of the 6th. Rises on local creeks, streams, and smaller rivers primarily led to flooded roads in Wood, Gilmer, and Ritchie Counties on the 4th, then runoff prompted minor flooding to develop on the Tygart Valley River at Mill Creek the morning of the 6th. Flooding came to an end once precipitation tapered off during the day.
episodes.209936: A front lifted into the area on the 3rd of March and then continued to ripple through the region over the next couple of days. Rain initially spread southwest to northeast across the area on the afternoon of the 3rd, then the focus of moderate to heavy rain became more confined to southeast Ohio and north central West Virginia during the evening and overnight hours. Another wave of showers pushed across the area after daybreak, but precipitation amounts were fairly light. A lull in precipitation occurred mid to late morning, then precipitation began streaming back into the area from the west during the afternoon. This resulted in a multitude of creeks and rivers to rise out of their banks in southeast Ohio, including the Little Muskingum River and Duck Creek. Local road closures also occurred as a result of nearby creeks and streams rising out of the banks and spilling onto the roadways. Flooding came to an end once precipitation tapered off on March 6th.
episodes.210076: On the evening of March 3, 2026, central Indiana experienced a wave of isolated severe weather fueled by record-breaking warmth and high humidity. The most significant severe report occurred in Hendricks County, where intense storms dropped 1 inch hail that was thick enough to completely cover road surfaces in areas like Avon. While the storms were scattered, they packed enough punch to create hazardous driving conditions and frequent cloud-to-ground lightning across the Interstate 74 corridor.||In addition to the hail, heavy rainfall led to localized flash flooding that caused significant disruptions in the southern suburbs. Near New Whiteland, rapid water accumulation forced the closure of several roads and led to a dangerous situation where a vehicle became stranded in floodwaters. This evening of activity was a precursor to a larger regional flooding event, as the 2 to 4 inches of rain saturated the ground and caused several local rivers to rise rapidly toward flood stage over the following 24 hours.
episodes.210077: Between the evening of March 3 and the late hours of March 4, 2026, a significant hydrologic event unfolded across central Indiana as a stalled frontal boundary interacted with a highly anomalous moisture profile. Driven by a robust 50-knot low-level jet, precipitable water values surged to nearly 1.30 inches���well above the 90th percentile for early March. While the Storm Prediction Center initially identified a low-probability severe threat, the environment was dominated by deep-layer moisture transport and training convective elements, leading to widespread 48-hour rainfall totals of 4 to 6 inches.
episodes.210078: During March 3 to March 7, 2026, large surface high pressure from the southeastern United States into the Atlantic focused a broad fetch of Gulf moisture northward into the Midwest.  A quasi-stationary frontal boundary near the Ohio Valley provided lift and focused, at times heavy rainfall over much of central Indiana, especially along the valley of the East Fork White River, and its tributaries northeast of Columbus through east-central central Indiana.||From the morning of the 3rd through dawn on the 4th, heavy rainfall over the watershed of the East Fork White's headwaters totaled mainly 2.00-3.75 inches.  Additional 1-day rainfall to dawn on the 5th, along the river's main stem from Columbus down through Martin County totaled generally 1.50-3.00 inches.  Further 2.5-day rainfall through late on the 7th was generally 1.00-2.00 inches along this main stem.  Overall 4.5-day rainfall totals were 4.00 to 6.00 inches for most portions of the entire East Fork White watershed.||Resultant widespread significant river flooding, including adjacent lowlands, from the Columbus area downstream through Jackson County, Lawrence County, and Martin County necessitated multiple water rescues.   Four persons over three counties perished when swept away by flood waters from the 6th to the 9th - three in motor vehicles and one in an airboat that encountered mechanical failure.
episodes.210213: A stationary front stalled out across Ohio and Indiana, sparking showers and thunderstorms along the boundary. Some of the storms produced locally heavy rainfall, resulting in instances of flash flooding.
episodes.210284: Severe thunderstorms with large hail fell across portions of southwest Missouri during the morning of March 4th. Additional thunderstorms with large hail fell across southern Missouri during the evening of March 4th. The two rounds of thunderstorms produced a swatch of 2-4 inches of rainfall from Cassville to Springfield to Salem. This rainfall caused localized flooding.
episodes.210471: A cold front moved into northern Arkansas from Missouri during the afternoon to evening timeframe on March 4, 2026 leading to the development of isolated thunderstorms. A few thunderstorms became severe and produced large hail.
episodes.210602: A mid-level shortwave trough, moving east across the Texas Panhandle, instigated scattered thunderstorms across western and northern Oklahoma during the early morning of the 4th. While much of this activity remained north of a surface boundary (i.e., elevated), sufficient instability and wind shear allowed for occasional storm intensification and organization. Large hail occurred in Harper County.
episodes.210812: A slow-moving front and a handful of upper level disturbances brought multiple rounds of showers and thunderstorms to North and Central Texas March 4 through 7, resulting in hail and flash flooding in some cases.
episodes.210974: Strong thunderstorms developed during the morning of the 4th across portions of eastern Oklahoma, as an upper level disturbance approached the region. The strongest thunderstorm produced hail to penny size.
episodes.210997: On the night of the 3rd and 4th of March, an upper level system moved in to the combined Panhandles sparking a line of thunderstorms running southwest to northeast across the central Texas Panhandle. The southern most storm developed into a severe storm that dropped hail up to 2 in diameter across Potter and Randall County.  On the evening of the 5th of March increase moisture advection in the southeastern Panhandles provided instability for severe thunderstorms. This time in the southeastern Panhandles. One of these storms dropped hail up to 1.7 in Collingsworth County.
episodes.212342: A strong surface high pressure system over the Atlantic Ocean produced a tight pressure gradient across the northeastern Caribbean during early March 2026. This pattern resulted in breezy to windy conditions across Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands, with several observing stations reporting wind gusts in the low 30s mph.

events.narrative: A large volume of hail which covered the roadways.
Standing water caused vehicles to become stranded on roads with at least one road closed by the high water.
The report was relayed through mPING.
Ping pong ball sized hail fell on the west side of Amarillo.

Hail of mostly nickel to quarter size fell across the western and northwestern side of Amarillo. However, hail of two inches in diameter fell near I-40 and Coulter Street. In addition, hail of golfball size fell to the west-northwest of Amarillo.
Flooding observed on Stillwell Road and Pristine Pointe.
US 50 was closed in both directions due to flooding from N Locust Street to Powder Plant Road.
State Route 124 was closed due to flooding from State Route 7 to the Meigs and Vinton County border. A flooded yard was also observed in this area.
High water was observed on State Route 93 near the Sheriffs Office.
Lee Creek rose out of its banks around the town of Belleville.
Horn Creek exceeded its banks and flooded portions of Alice Road.
State Route 143 was closed from Old Landfill Road to Township Road 1004 due to flooding.

Flooding was observed at State Route 349 and Lake Alma Road, and State Route 160 was closed due to flooding between South Buffalo Street and State Route 324. During the afternoon of the 4th, a vehicle was observed in water up to the windows at the intersection of State Routes 160 and 349.
Flooding was observed on Smithville Road between Indian Fork and Moyers culvert.

The Shade River near Chester rose above a bankfull level of 16 feet on the morning of March 4th, then continued to rise to a crest around 19.2 feet on the morning of March 5th. The river then slowly receded through the day, returning below bankfull that evening. While the river was out of its banks, flooding of low sections of Scout Camp Road, the Sugar Run Creek Bridge, fields and low-lying areas adjacent to the river took place.
Hail to the size of half dollars occurred northwest of Turners.
Hail to the size of half dollars fell northwest of Turners.
Hail to the size of quarters fell in Sacville.
Hail to the size of quarters fell in Grovespring.
Beals Run was out of its banks with several inches of moving water impacting the first floor of businesses and homes on Millville Avenue.

Rain bands moving across central Puerto Rico produced gusty winds that downed a tree and a utility pole onto PR-156 near Bayamoncito. The fallen debris blocked the roadway near kilometer 41.1, resulting in a temporary road closure. Law enforcement managed the incident, and the roadway was later reopened. Nearby observations indicated winds between 15 and 22 mph, with locally stronger gusts within the rain activity estimated near 40 mph.
Quarter-sized hail fell in the community of Dodd City.

Clifty Creek, rose through minor flood stage late on the 4th in Columbus, which was amplified by additional isolated downpours during the afternoon that totaled mainly 0.10-0.50 inches.  Twelve homeless individuals and three dogs had to be water rescued from their encampment under the US Highway 31 bridge over Clifty Creek.
Quarter-sized hail fell near the town of Bull Shoals with a significant amount of hail falling leading to a few hail drifts.
Quarter-sized hail fell at the 911 dispatch office in Salem.
Emergency manager reported that the US-80 and Belt Line underpass north of Mesquite was closed both ways due to flooding.
Quarter-sized hail fell to the northeast of the town of Hardy via firefighter.
Emergency manager reported that Liberty Grove Road at Broadmoor Lane was closed due to flooding.
Emergency manager reported that Main Street between Highway 66 and Rowlett Road was closed due to flooding.
